name: Yara Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: The Work Futures Panel is independent and has no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Yara Quinn, 43, a senior loader operator at a large mine. I read the blast clearance and ground report, then move ore to the crusher; I use AI daily to summarize production figures, but I check the face before changing a route.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the job, and what comes home with you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like finding a way through a slow shift without rushing the next operator. My partner Willa works at a veterinary clinic; we have two school-age children, a mortgage and about four months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a small software tool can sort haul notices, but it cannot feel a loose belt through the floor. I use AI every day to summarize production figures, and I still ask the operator what the machine sounded like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My shift is mostly on a loader, and the card says pay carries on as it would have. My partner Willa works at a veterinary clinic; we have two children, a mortgage and about four months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the morning machine walk and let the software sort the haul notices for a month. I would compare its summary with the shift log before changing my routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my current job in this mild picture. Willa and I have enough saved to handle an ordinary bill, and the tool does not change the loader work much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What work task would you want to keep in a person’s hands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Willa to check the mortgage date and the children's activity fees before moving money. We could postpone replacing the old garden gate if a pay statement came in short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2029, 2032 or 2037 after thinking AI arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask another operator to compare one week of haul notices with the actual machine checks. If the summary leaves out a fault, I would keep a person responsible for the sign-off.

say: I would use a tool to sort **haul notices**, but it cannot feel a loose belt.
I still ask operators what the **machine sounded like**.
think: My shift is mostly on a **loader**, and pay carries on here.
I rely on Willa’s clinic wage and our **four-month reserve**.
do: Keep the morning machine walk and test the **haul summary** for a month.
Compare it with the shift log before changing my **routine**.
feel: I feel **calm** about my current job in this mild picture.
S0.quote: I still ask the operator what the machine sounded like.
fieldNote: Yara uses AI daily for summaries but checks them against **operator knowledge**.
Her partner works outside mining, and the family has **four months saved**.
She sees no immediate threat to her own **shift** in the plateau case.

steps.text: Compare AI production summaries with shift logs
Keep the loader walk on every morning shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that software will handle more planning and booking, while robots take longer to reach a loader. I would ask for targets that account for what happens at the face, not only the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I help assign machines and tidy production notes, so those parts of my lead work could move early. I still spend most shifts operating, but fewer planning hours could affect my overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd test the new planner with a spare crew and learn how to check its haul sequence. I would start a mine-paid course in belt and conveyor inspection if the mine still needs people to make those checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy, but I am willing to test a system once the crew can question it. My concern is losing overtime if management replaces a lead shift with software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What work task would you want to keep in a person’s hands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a person to judge belt wear and loose material at the face. A route plan cannot tell whether a conveyor is safe to run after a rough shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2029, 2032 or 2037 after thinking AI arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the planner with a real shift that had delays before using it alone. If the sequence fails on a difficult day, I would record what the machine and crew actually needed.

I worry fewer planning hours could reduce my **overtime**.
do: Test the planner with a spare crew and learn its **haul sequence**.
Start belt-inspection training if the mine still needs **human checks**.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the system, and worry about losing overtime.
S1.quote: I feel uneasy, but I am willing to test a system once the crew can question it.
fieldNote: Her planning duties face change before the mostly **physical loader work**.
Yara is open to testing tools but wants crews to question **recommendations**.
She worries the mine may remove a **lead shift** and its overtime.

steps.text: Test the planner with a spare crew

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI can take shift plans by 2028, while hands-on robots reach loaders around 2031. We need a paid route into other work before the mine reduces the operating roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI could take my planning notes immediately, and robots could reach my main work three years later. I use AI daily, but that does not tell me whether a robot will need an operator beside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask now for the mine's belt-system course dates and a list of jobs that use the certificate. In 2029, I would take the paid course and stay on the loader roster while I look for a real inspection opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is fast, and I feel anxious because the robot date is close enough to affect my next career move. Willa's clinic wage and our savings help, but we still rely on mine income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What work task would you want to keep in a person’s hands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Willa and I would check the course schedule against her clinic shifts and the children's school year. I would not use the reserve for travel until a paid place and a vacancy were confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2029, 2032 or 2037 after thinking AI arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If no inspection place opened in 2029, I would keep operating and ask the belt crew for a supervised practice shift. I would apply only when the mine posted an actual opening.

say: I expect thinking AI to take shift plans by **2028**, with loader robots around 2031.
I want a paid route into other work before the **roster shrinks**.
think: I expect AGI to take planning notes first, with robots reaching my **main work** later.
I do not know whether the robot will need a **person** beside it.
do: Ask now for belt-system **course dates** and linked jobs.
Take the paid course in 2029 while keeping my **loader roster**.
feel: Two years feels **fast**, and the robot date affects my next move.
S2.quote: I use AI daily, but that does not tell me whether a robot will need an operator beside it.
fieldNote: She separates daily AI use from the later **robot risk** to loader work.
Yara requires a paid course and posted **opening** before using family savings.
Willa’s clinic shifts and the children’s school year shape **timing**.

steps.text: Take the paid belt-system course in 2029
Apply for a posted inspection opening

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people five years gives us time to prepare for AGI in 2031, while loaders face robots around 2034. The mine should show the crew what physical jobs may remain after that date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shift plans and records may change first, but the loader work remains for a while. I could move into belt inspection, though a robot may eventually inspect the belt too, so I would not call it a safe career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the belt-system course over the next few years and ask the mine to let me lead a supervised inspection. In 2032, I would apply for a funded belt-inspection role if the work still needed a person on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the ending, though five years gives me time to check this path. I would rather find out early whether inspection is being automated than build a plan around a job title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What work task would you want to keep in a person’s hands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the inspection role involves handling a damaged belt or only reviewing images. The physical work might last longer, but I need the actual duties before I leave the loader.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2029, 2032 or 2037 after thinking AI arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2032, I would ask the maintenance lead which inspection tasks remain human and apply if a funded post existed. If robots already covered the work, I would keep operating and check other local employers.

say: I see five years to prepare before AGI in **2031**.
I want to know which physical jobs remain after robots around **2034**.
think: I expect shift records to change first, while loader work lasts **longer**.
I will not call belt inspection a **safe career** from the title alone.
do: Finish the belt-system **course** and lead a supervised inspection.
Apply in 2032 for a funded inspection role with **on-site work**.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but five years lets me test the path early.
S3.quote: I would not call it a safe career.
fieldNote: She sees belt inspection as a possible bridge, not permanent **protection**.
She asks whether physical handling remains or only **image review**.
Yara will not leave loader income without a **funded position**.

steps.text: Apply for a funded inspection role in 2032
Keep operating until the inspection post is confirmed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the decade helps if we start before AGI arrives in 2036. Loader robots around 2039 leave more time, but I would still check what work remains for people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 at AGI and 56 when robots follow, and I still need a wage. I can train toward conveyor inspection, but I expect those jobs to change too if robots can examine the belt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the belt course while staying on the loader roster and save a set amount each month. In 2037, I would apply for inspection work only if the mine still funded human shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The long warning feels manageable because I can train while I earn. I remain uneasy about the end point, since four months saved cannot cover years without wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What work task would you want to keep in a person’s hands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2037, our children will be young adults, and Willa and I would ask what training they want before paying for anything. I would help them compare apprenticeships with employers beyond the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2029, 2032 or 2037 after thinking AI arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine to review staffing once a year and check whether nearby construction firms still hire operators. I would consider moving only after a confirmed offer and a family budget review.

say: I think the decade helps if we start before **2036**.
I expect loader robots around **2039** to raise questions about work.
think: At 53 and 56, I will still need a **wage**.
I expect conveyor inspection could change too if robots examine **belts**.
do: Finish the belt course while keeping my **loader roster**.
Save monthly and apply in 2037 for funded **human shifts**.
feel: The warning feels **manageable**, but I remain uneasy about the endpoint.
S4.quote: I remain uneasy about the end point, since four months saved cannot cover years without wages.
fieldNote: Yara uses the decade to train while maintaining **current income**.
She expects the children to be young adults by **2037** and includes them in course choices.
She would move only after a confirmed offer from a nearby **employer**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me because shift planning could change before I know where the loader job goes. Paid training, a funded opening and time to plan with Willa would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I would want the mine to say when it will change the roster and which skills it will pay workers to learn. I can adjust quickly, but nobody should pretend a course guarantees work.

headlineQuote: I can adjust quickly, but nobody should pretend a course guarantees work.
portrait: Yara is a 43-year-old senior mine operator with a **technical diploma**.
She uses AI daily to summarize figures while checking the physical **mine face** herself.
Her partner works at a veterinary clinic; their mortgage and **four-month reserve** shape plans.
She pursues belt inspection but recognizes **robots** may eventually automate that work.
biggestWorry: The **two-year AGI** picture worries her because shift plans may change before she can retrain.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **training**, a funded opening and time to plan with Willa would help Yara.
